s00404.title: Lesson 1 / Introduction
s00404.text: A whole number is not enough to describe every quantity. Explore rational numbers, then recall the four operations.

s00405.title: A larger number family
s00405.text: A rational number has the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero. Natural numbers, whole numbers and integers can all be written in this form.

s00406.title: Multiply and divide
s00406.text: To multiply, multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators. To divide by a nonzero rational number, multiply by its reciprocal. Preserve the signs.

s00407.title: Worked calculation
s00407.text: ASTAR worked explanation: (-10/21) x (14/25) = -140/525 = -4/15. Compare the original worked calculation on printed page 4.

s00417.title: Checkpoint / 4 minutes
s00417.text: Work in your notebook. Read all source tiles before answering. SELECT opens the action menu to record your attempt. Answers are not automatically graded.

s00418.title: Recap / 3 minutes
s00418.text: Rational numbers include integers and fractions. A denominator cannot be zero. Multiplication uses numerator and denominator products; division uses the reciprocal.

s00419.title: Lesson complete
s00419.text: Explain the key idea in your own words. SELECT and choose Mark lesson complete. Additional original questions are available in lesson practice and the chapter assessment.

s00420.title: Lesson 2 / Introduction
s00420.text: Investigate what changes when you swap or regroup numbers. Compare addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.

s00421.title: Closure
s00421.text: Adding, subtracting or multiplying two rational numbers gives another rational number. Division requires a nonzero divisor. The book describes Q as not closed under division because zero belongs to Q.

s00422.title: Order and grouping
s00422.text: Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative. Subtraction and division do not have these properties in general. A counterexample is enough to disprove a general property.

s00423.title: Test a claim
s00423.text: ASTAR worked explanation: (1 - 2) - 3 = -4, while 1 - (2 - 3) = 2. Changing the grouping changes the result, so subtraction is not associative.

s00436.title: Checkpoint / 4 minutes
s00436.text: Work in your notebook. Read all source tiles before answering. SELECT opens the action menu to record your attempt. Answers are not automatically graded.

s00437.title: Recap / 3 minutes
s00437.text: Ask three different questions: Is the result in the set? Does order matter? Does grouping matter? Use a nonzero divisor whenever you divide.

s00438.title: Lesson complete
s00438.text: Explain the key idea in your own words. SELECT and choose Mark lesson complete. Additional original questions are available in lesson practice and the chapter assessment.

s00439.title: Lesson 3 / Introduction
s00439.text: Learn which numbers leave a value unchanged, which undo an operation, and how multiplication distributes across a sum.

s00440.title: Two identities
s00440.text: Adding zero leaves a rational number unchanged: a + 0 = a. Multiplying by one leaves it unchanged: a x 1 = a. Zero is the additive identity; one is the multiplicative identity.

s00441.title: Two inverses
s00441.text: A number and its additive inverse sum to zero. Nonzero rational numbers have reciprocals whose product with the original number is one. Zero has no reciprocal.

s00442.title: Distribute multiplication
s00442.text: ASTAR notation guide: a x (b + c) = a x b + a x c. The same pattern works with subtraction. The original worked example on page 19 uses 2/5, 1/2 and 3/4.

s00455.title: Checkpoint / 4 minutes
s00455.text: Work in your notebook. Read all source tiles before answering. SELECT opens the action menu to record your attempt. Answers are not automatically graded.

s00456.title: Recap / 3 minutes
s00456.text: Identity preserves a value; inverse takes it to the identity. Distributing multiplication can simplify a calculation. Never take the reciprocal of zero.

s00457.title: Lesson complete
s00457.text: Explain the key idea in your own words. SELECT and choose Mark lesson complete. Additional original questions are available in lesson practice and the chapter assessment.

s00458.title: Lesson 4 / Introduction
s00458.text: Locate positive and negative fractions on the number line. Then find more rational numbers between two given values.

s00459.title: Equal parts
s00459.text: Divide each unit into as many equal parts as the denominator requires. Count the parts using the numerator. Negative rational numbers lie to the left of zero.

s00460.title: Between two numbers
s00460.text: For distinct rational numbers a and b, their mean (a + b)/2 lies between them. Repeating the method gives more numbers. Equivalent fractions with larger denominators offer another method.

s00461.title: A first midpoint
s00461.text: ASTAR worked explanation: between 2 and 3 is (2 + 3)/2 = 5/2. Between 2 and 5/2 is 9/4. The original diagrams and calculations are on page 26.

s00477.title: Checkpoint / 4 minutes

s00478.title: Recap / 3 minutes
s00478.text: Use equal intervals on a number line. Between any two distinct rational numbers there are infinitely many rational numbers. A mean supplies one of them.

s00479.title: Lesson complete
s00479.text: Explain the key idea in your own words. SELECT and choose Mark lesson complete. Additional original questions are available in lesson practice and the chapter assessment.

s00480.title: Lesson 5 / Introduction
s00480.text: Read terminating and recurring decimals, then convert them back into rational numbers. Keep recurring bars visible in the original source.

s00481.title: Divide to get decimals
s00481.text: A rational number has a terminating decimal or a non-terminating recurring decimal. In a recurring decimal, a digit or group of digits repeats in the same order.

s00482.title: Period and periodicity
s00482.text: The repeating group is called the period. Its number of digits is the periodicity. For 0.12757575..., the period is 75 and the periodicity is 2.

s00483.title: Return to a fraction
s00483.text: ASTAR worked explanation: let x = 0.545454... . Then 100x = 54.545454... . Subtract x to obtain 99x = 54, so x = 54/99 = 6/11. The textbook method appears on page 33.

s00494.text: Distinguish a finite decimal from a repeating one. Use a power of ten for terminating decimals. For recurring decimals, align repeating digits, subtract and solve for the fraction.
